Homocysteine.  ​Homocysteine, an amino acid metabolite 
of methionine, is a risk factor for CVD. It was first observed 
that children who were deficient in cystathionine B synthase, 
the essential enzyme for the breakdown of homocysteine, had 
premature atherosclerosis in some blood vessels. Elevated to-
tal homocysteine (tHcy) independently increases the odds of 
stroke, especially in younger individuals (Towfighi et al, 2010). 
Although evidence suggests that homocysteine may promote 
atherosclerosis, no causal link has been established. Homocys-
teine levels are influenced strongly by genetic factors and diet. 
Giving supplemental vitamins B6 and B12, which lower homo-
cysteine levels, is being investigated actively as a treatment for 
CVD but as of now is not widely recommended.
Trimethylamine-N-oxide.  Trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO) 
is a gut biota-dependent metabolite that contributes to heart dis-
ease (Tang et al, 2013). It is produced by the liver after intestinal 
bacteria have digested animal protein. TMAO has been shown to 
predict cardiac risk in individuals not identified by traditional risk 
factors and blood tests.
